options_ranked.title: Accelerated Base Oil Hedging & Supplier Contract Renegotiation
options_ranked.description: Lock in Q3–Q4 base oil input costs through forward-purchase agreements or fixed-price supplier contracts, and renegotiate supplier terms to shift exposure away from spot pricing. This works entirely on the cost side, so it is fully compatible with the price-lock constraint. Scope: applies to the shared input across all declining products (Synthetic Blend, Conventional, Compressor, Hydraulic); no action needed on the timeframe buckets already within threshold.
options_ranked.rationale: The measurement-first diagnosis holds: uniform margin degradation across premium (-7.14pp), conventional (-6.61pp), and industrial (-5.86pp) grades is the signature of a shared input-cost shock, not selective demand or mix. The confirmed causal chain base_oil_cost → COGS → Gross Margin % is the most defensible edge in the register, and this option pulls it directly without touching any pricing constraint. The falsification test is explicit: if base oil spot prices did NOT rise in the affected window, the diagnosis shifts to distribution/manufacturing cost or a costing-methodology artefact, and hedging spend should be halted.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 30–90 days (first hedged procurement cycle flows into COGS)

arguments_for: Directly targets the confirmed COGS mechanism behind the portfolio-wide decline and requires no customer-facing action, so there is zero risk to the price-lock constraint.
Benefits every declining grade simultaneously because base oil is a shared input, giving the broadest coverage per dollar of effort.
arguments_against: Hedging locks in today's cost — if base oil prices fall, the business forgoes the downside and could underperform unhedged competitors.
Recovers future margin only; it cannot claw back the year-to-date loss already booked.
key_questions: What has base oil spot pricing actually done since 2026-006, and what fraction of current COGS variance does it explain?
What hedge ratio (50%, 75%, 100% of forward volume) matches the company's risk appetite?

implementation_triggers: Procurement confirms base oil spot cost rose materially in the affected window (validating the diagnosis)
Supplier or exchange offers forward pricing at or below current spot
prerequisites: COGS decomposition isolating base oil vs manufacturing vs distribution vs packaging contribution to the margin decline
Treasury/board authorization for commodity hedging instruments
Volume forecast by grade to size forward-purchase commitments

impact_estimate.basis: Base oil typically represents 45–60% of COGS in these formulations; halting or reversing 10–15% of input-cost inflation via hedging recovers 3.5–5.8pp of the 7.14pp headline decline across the portfolio, since the input is shared by all affected grades.

key_assumptions.assumption: Base oil is the primary COGS component driving the decline, rather than distribution, packaging, or manufacturing cost.
key_assumptions.provenance: Confirmed register: base_oil_cost, distribution_cost, manufacturing_cost, and packaging_cost all sum into COGS; the specific attribution to base oil is checkable against the account-category COGS decomposition for 2026-006 onward.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forward pricing at or below current spot is available for the required volumes.
key_assumptions.provenance: Supplier quotes and the base oil forward curve obtained within the first two weeks of procurement outreach.

key_assumptions.assumption: The input-cost inflation is persistent enough (multi-quarter) that hedging pays off rather than locking in a peak.
key_assumptions.provenance: Base oil spot price remaining at or above current levels for two consecutive quarters would be consistent with this; a sustained fall would falsify it.

options_ranked.title: Renewal-Cycle Cost-Pass-Through Escalators + Base Oil Forward Contracting
options_ranked.description: Two commercial levers applied strictly outside the price-lock window: (1) layer a 3–5% documented cost-pass-through escalator into Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil contracts at their natural renewal points and into all new business — explicitly NOT applied mid-quarter to anchor accounts under lock; (2) open procurement negotiations for 6–12 month base oil forward contracts to stabilize input cost. Scope: targets Synthetic Blend (-7.14pp) and Conventional (-6.61pp), the two largest drivers; timeframe buckets already within threshold need no intervention.
options_ranked.rationale: Revenue-and-margin architecture directly addresses both sides of the ratio: the confirmed net_revenue↔gross_margin_pct relationship via escalators, and the confirmed base_oil_cost→COGS component via hedging. The original proposal's language about 'bypassing' the price-lock has been removed: escalators here apply prospectively at contract reset and to new business only, keeping the constraint intact. Escalators indexed to a published base oil benchmark also depoliticize the increase in renewal negotiations.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 60–120 days (first renewal cohort plus first hedged procurement cycle)

arguments_for: Attacks both the numerator and denominator of the margin ratio simultaneously, targeting the two products responsible for the largest deltas (-7.14pp and -6.61pp).
Indexation clauses create durable protection against future input-cost cycles, not just recovery of this one.
arguments_against: Recovery is gated by the renewal calendar — accounts deep inside their lock window contribute nothing until reset, so realized uplift may lag the estimate.
Escalators risk share loss to competitors who absorb the cost inflation, particularly in the price-sensitive Value category which is itself down 6.42pp.
key_questions: What share of Synthetic Blend and Conventional revenue comes up for renewal in the next two quarters?
What is the demand elasticity on renewal accounts if a 3–5% escalator is introduced?

implementation_triggers: Renewal calendar shows ≥25% of affected-product revenue resetting within 6 months
Base oil forward curve is flat or backwardated, making forward contracting economical
prerequisites: Legal confirmation of exactly which accounts and periods the price-lock clause covers, before any escalator language is drafted
Documented base oil cost inflation evidence pack for renewal negotiations
Renewal calendar mapped by product and account

impact_estimate.basis: A 3–5% net revenue uplift via renewal escalators on the largest driver (Synthetic Blend, -7.14pp), plus 1–2pp COGS relief from forward contracting, translating to 3.5–5.2pp blended Gross Margin % recovery against the observed decline.

key_assumptions.assumption: Renewal-cycle and new-business repricing falls outside the scope of the anchor-account price-lock clause.
key_assumptions.provenance: Legal review of the anchor contracts confirming the lock covers mid-quarter list changes only, not renewal resets.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers will accept a 3–5% documented cost-pass-through escalator without material volume defection.
key_assumptions.provenance: Renewal-cohort retention and volume in the 90 days following the first escalated renewals.

key_assumptions.assumption: Base oil cost inflation is the dominant COGS driver behind the margin decline.
key_assumptions.provenance: Confirmed causal register: base_oil_cost is an account_category component of COGS, and COGS movements directly move Gross Margin %; the synchronized decline across all oil grades is consistent with a shared input-cost driver.

flagged_side_effects: The original proposal framed escalators as a way around the anchor-account price-lock; as restated, escalators apply only at contract renewal and to new business, and any anchor account still inside its lock window is explicitly excluded until reset.

options_ranked.title: Portfolio Repositioning: Shift Volume Toward Structurally Higher-Margin Formulations
options_ranked.description: Treat the input-cost squeeze as potentially structural rather than a recoverable variance: reduce promotional intensity on Synthetic Blend and reallocate 30–40% of its volume toward higher-margin formulations (e.g., High Mileage) within the synthetic family over 3–12 months. IMPORTANT consistency caveat: the margin decline is portfolio-wide — the data does not confirm that the target formulations escaped the same COGS compression. Step 1 is therefore a margin verification of the target SKUs; the volume shift proceeds only where a verified 200–300bp structural margin premium survives the current cost environment. Segments and periods already within threshold are out of scope.
options_ranked.rationale: This questions the frame the other options optimize inside: if base oil inflation is a permanent category condition and pricing is contractually constrained, the participation question — how much low-margin volume the business should carry — matters more than variance recovery. The flagged concern that this reduces premium mix is addressed directly: the reallocation is WITHIN the premium/synthetic family (Synthetic Blend → higher-tier formulations), which raises rather than lowers effective premium mix; the unconfirmed premium-mix↔margin relationship is treated as a hypothesis to verify in Step 1, not asserted as fact.

arguments_for: Builds a margin structure that is robust to permanent input-cost inflation instead of betting on commodity prices reverting.
Reduces exposure to the worst-hit price bands — the Value category (-6.42pp) — without requiring any constrained price action.
arguments_against: The target formulations may be suffering the same COGS compression, in which case the shift moves volume without moving margin — the data shows every named product declined, so the premium is unverified.
Volume reallocation risks share loss in Synthetic Blend that is hard to reverse if the cost shock proves cyclical rather than structural.
key_questions: What are the CURRENT (post-shock) gross margins of the target formulations, and does a genuine premium survive?
Is the base oil cost rise structural (multi-year supply shift) or cyclical (spot volatility)?

implementation_triggers: Base oil costs remain elevated for two consecutive quarters, indicating structural rather than cyclical pressure
Target-formulation margin verification confirms a ≥200bp premium over Synthetic Blend in the current cost environment
prerequisites: SKU-level current-period margin analysis of candidate target formulations (High Mileage, full synthetic) to confirm the premium holds post-shock
Demand-side assessment of customer willingness to trade up within the synthetic family
Structural-vs-cyclical determination on base oil pricing

impact_estimate.basis: Reallocating 30–40% of Synthetic Blend volume to formulations carrying a verified 200–300bp margin premium yields 2.5–4.2pp of blended margin recovery — deliberately partial, since full recovery of the 7.14pp decline requires cost-side or pricing action this option does not take.

key_assumptions.assumption: Higher-tier synthetic formulations retain a 200–300bp structural margin premium over Synthetic Blend even under current input-cost conditions.
key_assumptions.provenance: Current-period SKU-level margin report for the target formulations showing a ≥200bp spread over Synthetic Blend's 20.64%.

key_assumptions.assumption: The base oil cost increase is structural (persistent multi-quarter), justifying portfolio change over tactical recovery.
key_assumptions.provenance: Base oil price staying elevated for two consecutive quarters would be consistent with this; reversion would falsify it.

key_assumptions.assumption: A within-family upshift raises rather than lowers premium mix, so the (unconfirmed) premium-mix-to-margin relationship works in this option's favor.
key_assumptions.provenance: The premium_mix↔margin link is an unconfirmed industry prior; blended margin tracking during the pilot reallocation would confirm or falsify the mechanism.

flagged_side_effects: Concern raised in review: moving volume away from Synthetic Blend, a premium product, could reduce the premium share of the portfolio and work against margin. Addressed by restricting the reallocation to WITHIN the synthetic family (upshift, not downshift) and gating execution on Step-1 verification that the target formulations' margin premium actually survives the current cost environment.

solutions.recommendation_rationale: The margin decline is synchronized and proportional across Synthetic Blend (-7.14pp), Conventional Engine Oil (-6.61pp), and Compressor Oil (-5.86pp) — the signature of a shared input-cost shock flowing through the confirmed base-oil-to-COGS-to-margin chain, not selective pricing erosion. Cost-side hedging is the only lever that addresses that mechanism for every affected grade simultaneously while carrying zero exposure to the anchor-account price-lock, making it the right first move; the renewal-escalator play should follow as renewal windows open, and the portfolio repositioning should be held pending its Step-1 margin verification.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross Margin % has dropped 7.14 points to a current level of 20.64 year-to-date versus prior year-to-date, with the blended portfolio margin falling from 34.43% to 29.94% (-4.49pp, -13.0%).
problem_reframe.complication: The compression is not isolated: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (-7.14pp), Conventional Engine Oil (-6.61pp), Compressor Oil (-5.86pp) and the Value category (-6.42pp) all degraded simultaneously and proportionally — a pattern consistent with a portfolio-wide COGS input shock (base oil) rather than selective discounting or mix drift. Meanwhile a contractual price-lock on Lubricants anchor accounts blocks mid-quarter list price recovery, forcing the entire margin absorption onto the cost side. Timeframe buckets outside the affected window remain within threshold, so the squeeze is period-concentrated starting around 2026-006.
problem_reframe.question: Which combination of cost-side hedging, renewal-cycle pricing architecture, and portfolio repositioning best recovers Gross Margin % without breaching the anchor-account price-lock?
key_assumptions: The synchronized decline across premium and value tiers indicates a shared COGS driver (base oil / distribution) rather than tier-specific demand erosion.
The price-lock applies to mid-quarter list changes on anchor accounts, not to renewal-cycle repricing outside the lock window or to new business.
The margin decline began in 2026-006 and persists through the current period rather than being a one-period artifact.

unresolved_tensions.tension: Hedging locks in current base oil costs, while the renewal-escalator play prices in continued inflation — if base oil prices fall, the two levers compound into over-recovery and competitive vulnerability on price.
unresolved_tensions.requires: CFO and Head of Procurement to set a hedge ratio (recommend 50–75%, not 100%) and an escalator cap tied to a published base oil index before either program launches (target: end of Week 2).

unresolved_tensions.tension: The portfolio repositioning treats the cost shock as permanent while the hedging and escalator options treat it as recoverable — committing to volume reallocation before the structural-vs-cyclical question is answered risks irreversible share loss in Synthetic Blend.
unresolved_tensions.requires: Head of Strategy to deliver a structural-vs-cyclical determination on base oil pricing, using two quarters of forward-curve and supply data, before any Synthetic Blend volume reallocation is approved (target: end of Q3).

blind_spots: The COGS decomposition attributing the decline specifically to base oil (vs distribution, packaging, or manufacturing cost — all confirmed COGS components) has not been performed; all three hypotheses assume base oil is dominant.
No customer- or channel-level margin view was analyzed — a concentrated discounting problem at one large account could mimic a portfolio-wide cost shock in product-level data.
Competitor response is unmodeled: if rivals absorb the input inflation, escalators and reduced Synthetic Blend promotion could both leak share.

A costing-methodology change (e.g., overhead allocation reset at the start of the fiscal year, coinciding with the 2026-006 onset) could inflate measured COGS without any real cost shock — the measured number has not been ruled out as an artefact.
next_steps: Direct Finance team to complete an account-category COGS decomposition (base oil vs manufacturing vs distribution vs packaging) for 2026-006 onward, confirming the dominant cost driver (by end of Week 1).
Instruct Head of Procurement to obtain base oil forward quotes and supplier fixed-price proposals for Q3–Q4 volumes (by end of Week 2).
Assign General Counsel to document the exact scope of the anchor-account price-lock clause — accounts, duration, and whether renewal-cycle escalators are permitted (by end of Week 1).
Task Commercial Operations with mapping the renewal calendar for Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil contracts, quantifying revenue resetting within 6 months (by end of Week 2).

Commission Product Finance to produce current-period margin analysis of High Mileage and full-synthetic SKUs, verifying whether a ≥200bp premium over Synthetic Blend survives the cost shock (by end of Week 3).

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Customer Profitability Lens
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin compression in Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil is driven by a combination of elevated base oil input costs (COGS pressure) and unfavorable mix shift toward lower-margin Value category products, masking any premium product volume gains. The 7.14pp and 6.61pp declines in the two largest contributors suggest structural COGS inflation rather than pricing power erosion alone.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%), the largest single product driver, while Value category margin fell 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), indicating simultaneous pressure on both premium and budget tiers—consistent with input cost inflation rather than selective channel or customer mix shift

Conventional Engine Oil declined 6.61pp (25.77% → 19.16%), showing near-parity with Synthetic Blend degradation, suggesting commodity base oil cost increases are affecting the entire lubricant portfolio uniformly

Compressor Oil margin declined 5.86pp, confirming the margin compression is portfolio-wide across oil types, not isolated to one SKU or customer segment, pointing to shared COGS driver (base oil procurement or distribution cost)

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14pp on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven by unhedged base oil cost inflation passing through COGS faster than selling prices can adjust due to contractual price-lock constraints. The 6.61pp delta on Conventional Engine Oil suggests a portfolio-wide input-cost shock rather than mix or volume effects. Premium product margin degradation while locked into fixed pricing indicates raw material cost (base oil) as the primary mechanism.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%) YTD, with Conventional Engine Oil declining 6.61pp (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating synchronized cost pressure across oil grades rather than selective demand or discounting.

Value category (which anchors lower-priced SKUs) declined 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), consistent with base oil cost pass-through affecting all tiers; premium mix shift alone would not degrade margin uniformly across price bands.

Principal constraint explicitly blocks mid-quarter price increases on Lubricants anchor accounts, creating a timing mismatch: input costs rising while revenue price points are frozen, forcing margin absorption entirely on the COGS side.
